feed.title: Practice & Challenges — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: CP-Algorithms
entry.content:
An English translation and extension of the e-maxx.ru write-ups on competitive-programming algorithms, each topic with code and practice problems. Unlike problem-solving platforms it explains the algorithm itself in depth rather than serving problems.

https://cp-algorithms.com/

entry.title: SELinux Game
entry.content:
A scenario-based game for learning SELinux that you run on your own machine. It turns the usually dry topic of policy writing into practical debugging tasks. Unlike plain documentation, it teaches policy through debugging tasks.

https://selinuxgame.org/index.html

entry.title: Python Challenge
entry.content:
A riddle game where each level is solved with a bit of Python. Unlike exercise sites every puzzle hides the next level’s address — you cannot move on without solving it.

https://www.pythonchallenge.com/

entry.title: Python Koans
entry.content:
A repository that teaches Python by making failing tests (“koans”) pass one at a time. Unlike reading a tutorial you fix real tests, so feedback is immediate.

https://github.com/gregmalcolm/python_koans

entry.title: Pytudes
entry.content:
Peter Norvig’s short Python programs and notebooks on puzzles, algorithms and language. Unlike exercise sites each is an expert’s worked solution with the reasoning explained.

https://github.com/norvig/pytudes

entry.title: Snakify
entry.content:
A Python 3 course with 100+ exercises, coded in the browser. Unlike video courses a checker verifies your solution at once.

https://snakify.org/en/

entry.title: Awesome Code Review
entry.content:
A resource list for the practice of code review. Unlike tool lists, it collects not only review tools but also articles and guidelines on review culture.

https://github.com/joho/awesome-code-review

entry.title: Beecrowd
entry.content:
An online judge grading programming, mathematics and SQL problems automatically, formerly URI Online Judge. Unlike LeetCode it is learning- rather than interview-oriented, with plenty of beginner problems.

https://www.beecrowd.com.br/judge/en/

entry.title: Code Golf (Stack Exchange)
entry.content:
A community contest to solve a problem in the shortest possible code. Unlike algorithm sites the measure is code length rather than speed or correctness — it shows how far languages can be bent.

https://codegolf.stackexchange.com/

entry.title: CodePen Challenges
entry.content:
Front-end (HTML/CSS/JS) challenges with an embedded editor, each round on a new theme. Unlike algorithm sites the result is visual: there is no single right answer, just creative solutions.

https://codepen.io/challenges

entry.title: Daily Coding Problem
entry.content:
A service that emails one coding-interview problem every day. Unlike problem platforms it lands in your inbox — the point is building a habit; detailed solutions are paid.

https://www.dailycodingproblem.com/

entry.title: devChallenges.io
entry.content:
A challenge site that has you build web projects with realistic designs and requirements. Unlike random projects the community reviews the solutions.

https://devchallenges.io/

entry.title: GeeksforGeeks
entry.content:
A very broad article archive of algorithms, data structures and interview questions. Unlike single-topic sites it has a worked example for almost every CS topic.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org

entry.title: RealWorld
entry.content:
A spec whose same realistic app (Conduit) is built across different front-end and back-end stacks.

https://realworld.how

entry.title: Rosetta Code
entry.content:
A wiki showing the same small problem solved in hundreds of languages. Unlike single-language examples it shows side by side how a task differs across languages.

https://rosettacode.org/

entry.title: TodoMVC
entry.content:
Shows the same to-do app built in dozens of JavaScript frameworks. Unlike the frameworks’ own demos the functionality is held constant, so only the approach changes and you can compare them side by side.

https://todomvc.com

entry.title: TopCoder Arena
entry.content:
The classic arena for timed algorithm competitions (SRM). Unlike Codeforces it uses the SRM format: after the coding phase comes a challenge phase where you score by feeding failing inputs to other people’s code.

https://arena.topcoder.com/

entry.title: UVa Online Judge
entry.content:
A classic online judge auto-grading hundreds of contest problems. Unlike newer platforms, it is the archive the problem lists of the Competitive Programming (Halim) book are built on.

https://onlinejudge.org/

entry.title: Python Tutor
entry.content:
Steps through code drawing stack frames and heap objects. Unlike a classic debugger it visualises memory — nothing explains reference semantics, scope and mutable default arguments as clearly.

https://pythontutor.com/

entry.title: AlgoDS
entry.content:
Java implementations of algorithms and data structures. Unlike textbook pseudocode, each is real, readable, working code with its tests.

https://github.com/sherxon/AlgoDS

entry.title: Algorithm Design Canvas
entry.content:
A stepwise framework for approaching an interview algorithm problem — constraints, examples, brute force, optimise, test. Method instead of panic.

https://www.hiredintech.com/algorithm-design

entry.title: AtCoder
entry.content:
A Japan-based contest platform whose beginner rounds (ABC) are more approachable for newcomers than Codeforces.

https://atcoder.jp/

entry.title: Big-O Cheat Sheet
entry.content:
A single colour-coded table of time and space complexity for data structures and sorting algorithms. Unlike a textbook it shows everything at a glance — the last look before an interview.

https://bigocheatsheet.com/#

entry.title: Big-O Yanılgıları
entry.content:
A piece correcting common misunderstandings of big-O notation. Unlike standard explanations, it targets subtle errors directly, such as conflating worst case with average case.

https://ssp.impulsetrain.com/big-o.html

entry.title: Bit İşlemleri Numaraları
entry.content:
A collection of common bit-level tricks — the patterns that turn up in low-level optimisation and interview questions.

https://gist.github.com/dideler/2365607

entry.title: CodeAbbey
entry.content:
A problem sequence starting at the very easiest and climbing gradually — a far gentler curve than the contest platforms for absolute beginners.

https://www.codeabbey.com

entry.title: CodeChef
entry.content:
A competitive algorithm platform with regular contests, difficulty-tagged problems and published editorial solutions. Unlike Codeforces, it offers learning paths and practice sections aimed at beginners.

https://www.codechef.com

entry.title: Codeforces
entry.content:
The busiest competitive programming platform, with regular rounds and a rating system. Problems run harder than LeetCode and lean heavily mathematical.

https://codeforces.com

entry.title: CodeGym
entry.content:
A practice-heavy course teaching Java through 1,200 hands-on tasks, with every solution checked automatically. Unlike video courses, it is tasks rather than theory: you advance by writing code.

https://codegym.cc/

entry.title: Coderbyte
entry.content:
An interview problem bank and assessment tool. Unlike LeetCode it offers video explanations of solutions and also hosts the assessment tool companies use to screen candidates.

https://coderbyte.com/

entry.title: CodeSignal
entry.content:
A skills assessment and interview platform that produces a standardised score you can send to several companies. The single assessment is the difference from sitting a separate test for every employer.

https://app.codesignal.com

entry.title: Codility
entry.content:
The assessment platform companies use for technical screening, with a practice section open to candidates. Its difference from other problem sites is that it mirrors the format of real screening tests — you see the exam environment before the exam.

https://app.codility.com/programmers/

entry.title: CodinGame
entry.content:
A platform that has you solve programming puzzles with a game theme, showing your code’s result in a game scene. Unlike dry problem sets it animates your solution visually.

https://www.codingame.com/

entry.title: Competitive Programmer’s Handbook
entry.content:
A free handbook for competitive programming, from basic algorithms to advanced techniques. Against academic algorithm books it is contest-oriented: it hands you an implementable template rather than a proof.

https://cses.fi/book.html

entry.title: CryptoHack
entry.content:
Teaches cryptography by breaking it, with each level exploiting a real weakness. Unlike a theory course it teaches from the attacker’s side — the applied counterpart.

https://cryptohack.org/

entry.title: freeCodeCamp
entry.content:
A complete free curriculum with in-browser exercises and free certificates. Its capstone projects make you build real applications rather than stopping at drills.

https://www.freecodecamp.com

entry.title: Google Interview Warmup
entry.content:
A practice tool where you answer interview questions aloud and get AI feedback. Unlike coding-interview sites, it focuses on behavioural and role questions, highlighting the key terms in your answer.

https://grow.google/certificates/interview-warmup/

entry.title: HackerEarth
entry.content:
Combines contests with hiring assessments — companies run technical screening here. Unlike HackerRank, it is strong on hosting hackathons.

https://www.hackerearth.com

entry.title: HiredInTech
entry.content:
Structured courses for system-design and algorithm interviews. Unlike problem banks it teaches method rather than questions — a framework for working a problem step by step; the content is old but the framework holds.

https://www.hiredintech.com/

entry.title: InterviewBit
entry.content:
Gamified interview preparation. Unlike LeetCode’s open problem pool, topics are ordered by dependency, each building on the last.

https://www.interviewbit.com
